A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same TQA robustness study. Their text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite the changed title and substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v2 reports original evaluations of language models on WTQ, TAT-QA, and SCITAB, including perturbation, few-shot, model-size, and table-complexity results.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical evaluations and adds original attention-entropy correlation analyses across models, datasets, layers, and heads.

M1.justification: The QA models, prompting approach, and structural/value perturbation procedures remain unchanged. The new attention diagnostics do not introduce a modified QA architecture, training objective, or inference algorithm.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate WTQ, TAT-QA, and SCITAB under the same structural and no-table conditions, with value perturbations restricted to WTQ. The attention analyses reuse this existing coverage.

E2.justification: Table 3 retains the same twelve Llama2, Llama3, Mistral, and Mixtral base/chat/instruction variants. Their participation in the corresponding benchmark comparisons is unchanged; the new attention analyses use existing models.

E3.justification: Section 4 and Appendix H introduce an evaluation design comparing original and perturbed attention entropy, computing head-level and layer-level correlations with EM changes across five structural perturbations. The original sample counts, model configurations, few-shot settings, and EM/VP/Emd metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds attention–performance association studies, layer sensitivity analysis, checks across eighteen model–dataset pairs, and contrasting individual-head case studies. The earlier table-complexity and few-shot analyses remain available in the appendices.

E5.justification: v3 introduces Spearman correlation estimation and significance reporting, including p = 0.037 in Section 4.1. Existing benchmark error-bar displays are retained; no additional run counts or seed protocol are disclosed.

E6.justification: v3 adds the reported attention-entropy/EM-degradation correlation of rho = 0.90 for Llama3-8B-Instruct on WTQ, layer/head correlation results, and cross-model results in Figure 16. The full benchmark table is unchanged from v2 Table 4 to v3 Table 1, and retained benchmark plots contain the same results.

T1.justification: New Appendix H supplies mathematical definitions of attention entropy, sink rate, Frobenius norm, and the norm difference between original and perturbed attention matrices. These extend the measurement definitions; no theorem, proof, or formal guarantee is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion add a central contribution linking attention-dispersion changes to performance degradation, with sensitivity claimed to peak in middle layers. Earlier claims about prompting, instruction tuning, scale, and domain bias are retained.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning attention disruption, middle-layer vulnerability, head stability, and entropy change as a broadly applicable robustness proxy. It also acknowledges that computational cost restricts attention analysis to small models; earlier limitations remain.

D1.justification: Appendices A–D retain the same prompt templates, ChatGPT-3.5 counterfactual generation, filtering instructions, sample-count disclosures, and exact model identifiers. No new software implementation, hardware, runtime, or code/data access information is supplied.

R1.justification: The introduction substantially reframes the research gap around internal attention mechanisms in structured tasks. It adds Clark et al. (2019), Barbero et al. (2025), and Zhao et al. (2024), while removing earlier citations including TaPas, StructGPT, and Chain-of-Table.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion are rewritten around attention analysis. Results are condensed and reordered, earlier model-size and instruction-tuning discussion moves to Appendix G.1, and a new main section and Appendix H reorganize the narrative.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn and gains an attention scatter plot; new attention heatmaps, layer plots, cross-model bars, and head-level scatters are added. v2 Table 4 becomes v3 Table 1, while v2 Figures 3–4 move to the appendices as v3 Figures 15 and 10. Several retained plots are resized.

improvement.justification: v3 preserves the benchmark evidence and adds useful exploratory attention analyses, significance reporting, and checks across eighteen model–dataset pairs. This improves diagnostic depth, but Section 4.1's causal interpretations and Appendix H.2's inference of head stability from weak correlation exceed what the presented correlations establish, limiting the overall gain.
